notes.definition: Microscopy is the use of microscopes to produce magnified images of cells and sub-cellular structures. Electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolving power than light microscopes, so they show cells in much finer detail.
explanation: Microscopy techniques have developed over time. The first light microscopes were made in the 1600s, when scientists such as Robert Hooke first saw and named 'cells'. Light microscopes improved over the next few hundred years, revealing nuclei, chloroplasts and bacteria. In the 1930s the electron microscope was invented. Instead of light, it uses a beam of electrons to form an image, and this gave biologists a completely new view of the inside of cells.

Two key ideas describe how good a microscope is. Magnification is how many times bigger the image is than the real object. Resolution (resolving power) is the ability to distinguish between two points that are close together: the higher the resolution, the more detail can be seen. A light microscope can magnify up to about ×1500 and can resolve objects about 200 nm apart. An electron microscope can magnify up to about ×2 000 000 and can resolve objects about 0.1 nm apart.

Light microscopes are cheap, small and easy to use, can show living cells and give colour images. Their limitation is resolution: structures smaller than about 200 nm, such as ribosomes, cannot be seen, and the internal structure of mitochondria and chloroplasts is unclear. Because electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolving power, biologists have been able to see and understand many more sub-cellular structures, such as ribosomes, the folded inner membranes of mitochondria and the internal membranes of chloroplasts, and to study plasmids in bacteria. Electron microscopes are large and expensive, and specimens must be dead because they are viewed in a vacuum.

You must be able to calculate magnification using: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object. This can be rearranged to find the real size (real size = image size ÷ magnification) or the image size (image size = magnification × real size). Both sizes must be in the same unit before you divide. Remember 1 mm = 1000 μm and 1 μm = 1000 nm. Magnification has no units, but it is written with a '×' sign, such as ×400. Very large or very small answers should be given in standard form, for example 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m.

For a light microscope, total magnification = eyepiece lens magnification × objective lens magnification. In required practical 1 you prepare a slide, such as onion epidermis stained with iodine solution, and view it with a light microscope. Always start with the lowest power objective, focus with the coarse focusing knob, then use the fine focusing knob, before moving to a higher power. Draw what you see with a sharp pencil, using clear, unbroken lines with no shading, add labels with straight ruled lines, and record the magnification or include a scale bar.
keyFacts: Magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object.
Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two points that are close together.
Electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolving power than light microscopes.
Light microscope: up to about ×1500, resolution about 200 nm; electron microscope: up to about ×2 000 000, resolution about 0.1 nm.
Electron microscopes allowed biologists to see and understand many more sub-cellular structures, such as ribosomes.
Light microscopes can be used on living specimens; electron microscope specimens must be dead.
Total magnification of a light microscope = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
Convert image size and real size to the same unit before calculating.
Required practical 1: use a light microscope to observe, draw and label plant and animal cells, including a magnification or scale bar.

keyTerms.definition: How many times bigger the image is than the real object.
The ability to distinguish between two points that are close together; the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as separate.
A microscope that uses light and glass lenses to form a magnified image.
A microscope that uses a beam of electrons to form an image, giving much higher magnification and resolution than a light microscope.
The lens you look through on a light microscope, usually ×10.
The lens close to the specimen on a light microscope; usually there are several with different magnifications such as ×4, ×10 and ×40.
A dye, such as iodine solution or methylene blue, that makes cells or structures show up more clearly.
A line on an image or drawing labelled with the real length it represents, used to work out real sizes.

equations.formula: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object
equations.units: no units (it is a ratio); I and A must be in the same unit

equations.name: Total magnification of a light microscope
equations.formula: total magnification = eyepiece lens magnification × objective lens magnification

workedExamples.title: Calculating magnification
workedExamples.question: A cell is 0.05 mm long. In a drawing, the cell is 20 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
steps: Both sizes are already in mm.
magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object = 20 ÷ 0.05.

workedExamples.title: Calculating real size with a unit conversion
workedExamples.question: A micrograph of a cell has a magnification of ×1500. The image of the cell is 45 mm long. Calculate the real length of the cell in μm.
steps: Rearrange: size of real object = size of image ÷ magnification.

workedExamples.title: Magnification in standard form
workedExamples.question: An electron micrograph shows a mitochondrion. The image is 36 mm long. The real mitochondrion is 1.2 μm long. Calculate the magnification and give it in standard form.
steps: Convert the image size into μm: 36 mm × 1000 = 36 000 μm.

workedExamples.title: Using a scale bar
workedExamples.question: On a micrograph, a scale bar 25 mm long represents 10 μm. A cell on the micrograph measures 50 mm. Calculate the real length of the cell.
steps: Find the magnification: 25 mm = 25 000 μm, so magnification = 25 000 ÷ 10 = 2500.
Real size = image size ÷ magnification = 50 000 μm ÷ 2500 = 20 μm.
Check: the cell is twice as long as the scale bar, so it is 2 × 10 μm = 20 μm.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think magnification and resolution mean the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact magnification is how much bigger the image is, while resolution is how much detail can be seen. Magnifying a blurry image more does not show more detail.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often divide image size by real size without converting to the same unit.
misconceptions.right: In fact both sizes must be in the same unit, for example both in μm, before you divide. Otherwise the answer is wrong by a factor of 1000 or more.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think electron microscopes are better for every job.
misconceptions.right: In fact light microscopes are better for viewing living cells, in colour, cheaply. Electron microscopes need dead specimens in a vacuum and are very expensive.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the real size is image size × magnification.
misconceptions.right: In fact real size = image size ÷ magnification. The real object is smaller than the image, so your answer should be smaller.

realWorld: Electron microscopes are used to study viruses, such as the coronavirus that causes COVID-19, which are far too small to be seen with a light microscope.
Hospital laboratories use light microscopes to examine blood smears and tissue samples to diagnose diseases such as anaemia, malaria and cancer.
Electron microscopy revealed the detailed structure of mitochondria and chloroplasts, helping scientists understand how respiration and photosynthesis work.
examTips: Learn magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object. AQA does not give you this equation, so you must recall it.
Always convert to the same unit first. Write the conversion as a separate line of working so you can get method marks even if the final answer is wrong.
Sense-check answers: a real cell should be micrometres in size, and a magnification is usually between ×40 and ×2 000 000.
When explaining why electron microscopes show more detail, say 'higher resolution' (or resolving power), not just 'higher magnification'.
For drawing questions in required practical 1, use a sharp pencil, clear continuous lines, no shading, ruled label lines that do not cross, and include the magnification or a scale bar.
Give answers in standard form when they are very large or very small, e.g. 3 × 10⁴ or 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m.
summary: Magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object.
Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two close points.
Electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes.
Electron microscopes revealed many more sub-cellular structures, such as ribosomes.
Light microscopes can show living cells in colour; electron microscopes need dead specimens.
Use the same units and give very large or small answers in standard form.
Required practical 1: prepare, stain, focus, then draw and label cells with a magnification or scale bar.

questions.question: Which equation is correct for calculating magnification?
options: size of real object ÷ size of image
size of image × size of real object
size of image ÷ size of real object
size of image − size of real object
markScheme: 1 mark: size of image ÷ size of real object
questions.explanation: Magnification is how many times bigger the image is, so you divide the image size by the real size. Dividing the other way round gives a number less than 1.

questions.question: Which type of microscope has the highest resolution?
options: Light microscope with a ×10 objective
Light microscope with a ×40 objective
Light microscope with a ×100 objective
Electron microscope
markScheme: 1 mark: electron microscope
questions.explanation: Electron microscopes have far higher resolving power than any light microscope. Changing the objective lens increases magnification, but a light microscope can never resolve details smaller than about 200 nm.

questions.question: Which sub-cellular structure can only be seen using an electron microscope?
options: Nucleus
Ribosome
Cell wall
Chloroplast
markScheme: 1 mark: ribosome
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are about 25 nm across, far smaller than the 200 nm resolution limit of a light microscope. The nucleus, cell wall and chloroplasts can all be seen with a light microscope.

questions.question: What is meant by the resolution of a microscope?
options: The ability to distinguish between two points that are close together
How many times bigger the image is than the object
How bright the image is
The size of the specimen being viewed
markScheme: 1 mark: the ability to distinguish between two points that are close together
questions.explanation: Resolution is about detail: how close two points can be and still be seen as separate. 'How many times bigger' is the definition of magnification.

questions.question:
A student uses a light microscope.
Table 1 shows the magnification of the lenses the student uses.
What is the total magnification?
markScheme: 1 mark: ×400
questions.explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 10 × 40 = 400. Adding them (×50) is a common mistake.

questions.question: How many micrometres (μm) are there in 1 millimetre (mm)?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1000
questions.explanation: 1 mm = 1000 μm. There are 1 000 000 μm in a metre, not in a millimetre.

questions.question: Why can ribosomes not be seen with a light microscope?
options: Ribosomes do not absorb electrons
Ribosomes are too small to be resolved: they are smaller than the light microscope's resolution
Ribosomes are destroyed by light
Ribosomes are only found in dead cells
markScheme: 1 mark: ribosomes are too small to be resolved by a light microscope
questions.explanation: Light microscopes cannot resolve objects smaller than about 200 nm, and ribosomes are about 25 nm. Ribosomes are present in living cells and are not destroyed by light.

questions.question:
A student prepares a slide of onion epidermis cells.
The student adds a drop of iodine solution to the cells.
Why does the student add iodine solution?
options: To kill bacteria on the slide
To stop the cells drying out
To increase the magnification
To stain the cells so that structures such as the nucleus show up clearly
markScheme: 1 mark: to stain the cells so that structures show up clearly
questions.explanation: Iodine is a stain that makes the nucleus and cell wall easier to see. It does not change the magnification, which depends only on the lenses.

questions.question: Which is a limitation of an electron microscope compared with a light microscope?
options: It has a lower resolution
It cannot magnify more than ×1500
It uses light, so small structures are blurred
Specimens must be dead because they are viewed in a vacuum
markScheme: 1 mark: specimens must be dead because they are viewed in a vacuum
questions.explanation: Electron microscopes need specimens to be in a vacuum, so living cells cannot be observed. They have higher resolution and magnification than light microscopes, and they use electrons, not light.

questions.question:
A red blood cell is 8 μm across. It is viewed using a light microscope at a magnification of ×400.
Calculate the size of the image in mm.
markScheme: 1 mark: image size = 400 × 8 = 3200 μm
1 mark: 3.2 mm
questions.explanation: Image size = magnification × real size = 400 × 8 = 3200 μm. Divide by 1000 to convert to mm: 3.2 mm.

questions.question:
A scientist measured the length of a mitochondrion in an electron micrograph.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the magnification of the micrograph.
markScheme: 1 mark: converts 15 mm to 15 000 μm
questions.explanation: Convert first: 15 mm × 1000 = 15 000 μm. Then 15 000 ÷ 1.5 = 10 000. In standard form this is ×1 × 10⁴.

questions.question: What does an electron microscope use to form an image instead of light?
markScheme: 1 mark: (a beam of) electrons
questions.explanation: Electron microscopes use a beam of electrons. This gives much higher resolution than light.

questions.question: Give two advantages of an electron microscope compared with a light microscope.
markScheme: 1 mark: higher magnification
1 mark: higher resolution / resolving power (so more detail / smaller structures such as ribosomes can be seen)
questions.explanation: Electron microscopes magnify much more and, crucially, have much higher resolution, so fine detail and tiny structures can be seen.

questions.question: Explain how electron microscopy has increased our understanding of sub-cellular structures.
markScheme: 1 mark: electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolution, so cells are seen in much finer detail
1 mark: so more sub-cellular structures could be seen / understood, e.g. ribosomes, internal structure of mitochondria or chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Higher resolution revealed structures that light microscopes cannot show, such as ribosomes, and the internal membranes of mitochondria and chloroplasts, helping biologists work out how these structures function.

questions.question: Give two advantages of using a light microscope rather than an electron microscope.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: cheaper; smaller / portable; easier to use; can view living specimens; images in colour; simpler specimen preparation
questions.explanation: Light microscopes are cheap and practical and can show living cells in colour, while electron microscopes need dead specimens in a vacuum.

markScheme: 1 mark: place slide on the stage and start with the lowest power objective lens
1 mark: use the coarse focusing knob to focus (moving the lens away from the slide), then the fine focusing knob
1 mark: switch to a higher power objective and refocus using the fine focusing knob only
questions.explanation: Starting at low power makes it easy to find the cells. Using only fine focus at high power avoids crashing the objective lens into the slide.

questions.question: Give three rules a student should follow when making a scientific drawing of cells seen through a microscope.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any three from: use a sharp pencil; clear, continuous (unbroken) lines; no shading or colouring; label lines drawn with a ruler and not crossing; include the magnification or a scale bar; draw only what is seen, in proportion; take up a good proportion of the space
questions.explanation: Scientific drawings must be clear and accurate. Shading and sketchy lines hide detail, and a magnification or scale bar lets others work out real sizes.

questions.question: What is meant by magnification?
acceptedAnswers: how many times bigger the image is
markScheme: 1 mark: how many times bigger the image is than the real object
questions.explanation: Magnification compares the size of the image with the size of the real object. It is not the same as resolution, which is about detail.

questions.question: Describe how a student could prepare a slide of onion epidermis cells and use a light microscope to observe, draw and label them.
markScheme: Indicative content:
peel a thin layer of epidermis from an onion with forceps (one cell thick so light passes through)
place it flat on a clean microscope slide in a drop of water
add a drop of iodine solution to stain the cells
lower a coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle to avoid air bubbles
place slide on the stage, start with the lowest power objective
focus with the coarse focusing knob, then the fine focusing knob
switch to a higher power objective and refocus with the fine focusing knob
draw with a sharp pencil, clear unbroken lines, no shading
label structures (cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus) with ruled lines
record the magnification (eyepiece × objective) or add a scale bar
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a logical, detailed method covering preparation, staining, focusing and drawing, which could be followed to give valid observations.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most main steps, but some detail missing or steps out of order.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): a few relevant steps with little detail or logical order.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A top answer follows the practical in order: prepare a thin layer, stain, add coverslip, focus from low to high power, then make a clear labelled drawing with magnification. Each step should include its reason where possible.

questions.question:
A scientist wants to (a) watch living cheek cells take up a dye and (b) study the structure of ribosomes.
Evaluate which type of microscope she should use for each task.
markScheme: Indicative content:
(a) light microscope
because the cells must be alive / electron microscope specimens are dead (in a vacuum)
light microscope shows colour so the dye can be seen
(b) electron microscope
because ribosomes are too small to be resolved by a light microscope (smaller than about 200 nm)
electron microscope has much higher resolution and magnification
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct choice for both tasks, each supported by a valid reason.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): correct choice for one or both tasks with little or no reasoning.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Neither microscope is best for everything. Living cells need a light microscope; tiny structures like ribosomes need the resolution of an electron microscope.
